content.thinking:
At 390px, the captions need more vertical space than I thought — the idle and expired states take up 60px while revealed and failed only need 40px, creating a 20px shift. My current `min-h-[2lh]` setting of 40px isn't sufficient, so I need to bump it to `min-h-[3lh]` at 60px to accommodate all four states. The clone measurement approach gave me misleading data since it was appended to the flex row parent, which changed its width context.

Looking at the actual detail text lengths across the three states — served at 57 characters, expired at 74, and revealed at 67 — they all render to 3 lines at the narrow 390px column width (around 266px after accounting for padding, label, and gap). Since text-sm gives a 24px line height, that's consistently 72px across all three. Setting `min-h-[3lh]` on the detail element would match the natural height at mobile with no wasted space, while at desktop it would reserve 72px where the natural height is only 48px — adding 24px of dead space but ensuring consistent layout.

The real question is whether that trade-off is worth it. The measured evidence shows the details already agree within each breakpoint without needing a minimum height constraint, but that's fragile if the copy changes. A `min-h-[2lh]` floor would be safer without adding dead space, though I should document this fragility somewhere — maybe in the test file where I can capture the measured heights and explain the reasoning.

For the caption, the math is clearer: at desktop it needs 40px minimum to prevent shift when copy shortens, and at mobile it needs 60px. So `min-h-[3lh]` is the right call for the caption, even though it reserves 20px of dead space at desktop.

Actually, a responsive approach makes more sense — `min-h-[3lh] sm:min-h-[2lh]` reserves 3 lines below 640px and 2 lines above, which matches the measured maximums exactly at those breakpoints. The risk is widths between those breakpoints might have different line counts, so I should check a mid-range width like 768px to make sure the reserve is sufficient everywhere.

Better yet, I can use the same ghost-stack technique I already applied to the button label — render the longest caption variant invisibly in the same grid cell so the slot always sizes to fit the tallest possible caption at any viewport width, no magic numbers needed. For the caption and detail, I'd stack invisible copies of all variants and let the grid size to the maximum, which is exact at every width. The DOM cost of a few extra hidden strings is negligible, but I need to make sure those ghost elements have `aria-hidden="true"` so they don't get announced by screen readers.

This might seem like over-engineering, but it's the difference between being stable at a couple of test widths versus being stable everywhere — and Eric was clear it needs to be stable. A simple `Slot` helper component that takes the active string and all variants, renders them stacked in a single grid cell, would be clean and self-documenting at around 15 lines, used twice. This eliminates the need for any min-height magic entirely.

Writing component code... I could have `readout` return the variants too, but `privateId` won't be known until after the fetch completes. A simpler approach: use actual strings where they're known and same-length placeholders for unknowns, though that's getting messy. Looking at my measurements though, all three details wrap identically across both widths (they're all 57-74 characters), and the `dd` already has a min-height floor, so the risk is actually pretty low. The real layout shift happens with the caption. So I'll apply the ghost-stack technique to just the caption—all four variants are static strings, which is perfect—and give the detail a responsive min-height based on measurements while keeping the copy lengths consistent.

The detail variants are nearly static too, with only the clock (fixed width) and two 8-character IDs varying. I can build ghost strings with fixed placeholder digits that match the exact length of the real ones, then export them from the copy file so they stay in sync and can't drift apart. That's worth testing. I'll just assert that the real detail length matches the corresponding ghost variant length—that's a clean way to catch any drift when copy gets edited. content.text:
Pushed — PR #364 now has 7 commits. 189/189 tests, typecheck and Biome clean.

## The three copy calls

**1. Silent failure → lighter alternative, in the caption slot.** `handleRebake` now catches, and the caption becomes *"the re-bake didn't come back. Try again?"* in `text-destructive`. Putting it in the caption rather than under the button means the failure costs zero height — no new line, and it inherits the live region so it's announced.

The wording promises nothing about what happened, deliberately: `updateTag` may have run before the response died, and the client genuinely can't know.

**2. Phase-C caption** → *"expiring an entry and refilling it are two different events. You just watched both."* Resets to the idle caption on the next re-bake, so the second pass reads correctly.

**3. Hero** → `bake #6bd42b51 · 11 Aug 2026, 08:26:57 UTC`, in three tiers: quiet label, vivid half-weight-up fingerprint, `tabular-nums` timestamp.

## On the layout shift

You were right that it jumped, and clicking through the phases wouldn't have found all of it — at 390px the caption is 3 lines for two variants and 2 for the others, a 20px hop I'd have shipped.

So rather than tune a magic number per breakpoint, each slot now renders its live string stacked over invisible copies of **every string it could hold**. The cell is always as tall as its true worst case, at whatever width the reader is actually at. The ghosts are `visibility: hidden` and `aria-hidden`, so they cost nothing in tab order, selection, or announcements.

Measured after: **one distinct panel height across all 11 variant/slot combinations** at 360, 390, 768 and 1280px. The fetch button is also always rendered (hidden when it doesn't apply) so the button row reserves its footprint, and the button labels stack the same way so nothing slides during the pending flash.

A test pins the placeholders — a clock is always `HH:MM:SS`, a bake id always 8 hex — so a copy edit that changes a detail's length without updating its ghost fails rather than silently un-reserving the space.

## Two things I did that you didn't ask for

**I found a WCAG failure and it was partly mine.** My first pass at the hero tiers put the `bake` label at **2.32:1**. Fixing it revealed the *pre-existing* streamed line was at **3.48:1** — also failing AA in light mode. Since I'd just changed line one's colour, leaving line two would have made them visibly mismatch as well as fail. Both now share one base colour: **4.74 / 4.56 / 4.74 light, 12.65 / 18.02 / 12.65 dark** — all clear.

That's a visual change to copy you'd previously signed off, so flag it if you'd rather keep the old weight; it's one class.

**The `·` separator** is `aria-hidden` and at 40% opacity — decorative, so exempt from the contrast rule, but say the word if it reads too faint.

content.thinking:
I'm looking at this line and noticing the ambiguity around which hash is which — the past tense "you saw" refers to a hash that's no longer visible, while "the cache kept" points to the one currently displayed on screen, but a reader might not immediately grasp which is which or understand the temporal relationship between them. The two 8-character hex values add to the confusion without clear context about what they represent.

The word "kept" is also imprecise — the cache didn't retain something that already existed, it generated a new one, so "stored" or "generated" would be more accurate. And structurally, the sentence has two separate jobs: the label "served" and the detail "from the static shell" are doing different work, which makes the whole thing feel disjointed.

The core issues are that it's unclear which hash is currently on screen, the verb choice is misleading, and the two hashes need to have clearly distinct roles — one is ephemeral and gone, the other is persistent and present. I'm considering whether the label itself might need to change to better capture what's happening in this phase.

I'm drafting a few approaches: one that explicitly names where each hash lives, another that anchors to the visible stamp, and a third that restructures the layout entirely into two parallel rows so the hashes and their roles are unmistakably clear.

The two-row option is the strongest for clarity — parallel structure with aligned hashes beats prose with two hex strings. The trade-off is layout stability: I'd need to reserve space for two rows across all phases, leaving dead space in phases A and B. But actually, the detail could just be two lines internally instead, which the StableSlot already accommodates at desktop, so phase C's longer detail wouldn't add extra overhead.

Now I'm considering a sequential narrative approach for the detail text — something like "rendered for you and thrown away, then replaced for everyone" — which creates clear cause-and-effect and uses vivid language that matches what actually happened.

I'm also exploring whether I can drop one of the hash codes entirely since the current one is already visible in the stamp above, leaving just the departed hash to identify. That would simplify the line and let "This one" point directly at the stamp without forcing the reader to parse two hex strings.

But there's tension here — showing both hashes side-by-side is what makes the evidence undeniable, even if it's harder to read. Dropping one means the reader has to trust their memory of what they saw, which they can't actually verify either way.

So the real win is keeping both hashes but making their distinct roles crystal clear. I could label them inline with terse notation like `yours: #1e472bda (gone) · everyone's: #a020a685 (above)`, which scans quickly and matches the page's existing style. Or I could split them across two lines in the definition list, with each hash getting its own explanatory phrase — that gives the strongest clarity without losing the comparison that makes the whole thing convincing.

I'm settling on four distinct options to present, each with clear tradeoffs. The minimal fix just corrects the tense and wording. The second points directly at which hash is on screen. The third uses terse role labels in parallel. The fourth goes full two-row clarity. I should also consider whether the label itself — currently "served" — reads better as something like "compare" or "kept" or "result" depending on which option I'm showing. Option 4 uses two rows instead of one to show both hashes with their full context — you see what was rendered just for you versus what everyone gets. The trade-off is adding a row to the display list in one phase, though I could reserve space for it across all phases to keep the layout consistent.

Let me estimate the actual cost here. At desktop, reserving that extra row would be around 24 pixels — not free, but not a deal-breaker either. I should present all four options with this layout consideration in mind and probably recommend option 2, or option 4 if maximum clarity matters more than the height cost.

I need to verify that whichever option I choose has matching ghost placeholder lengths in the test suite.…

content.text:
Current line, phase C:

> `served`    from the static shell — you saw #1e472bda, the cache kept #a020a685

Three things work against it. Two 8-character hex strings sitting side by side look nearly identical at a glance. Nothing tells you **which one is the big hash above** — the reader has to infer it. And *"kept"* is subtly wrong: the cache didn't retain something it already had, it stored the replacement.

Four directions, roughly in order of how much they change:

---

**1. Minimal repair** — same shape, honest verbs

> `served`    from the static shell — you were shown #1e472bda, the cache stored #a020a685

Fixes "kept", and "were shown" makes it something done *to* you rather than something you did. Cheapest option. Still leaves the reader working out which hash is on screen.

---

**2. Point at the stamp** *(my recommendation)*

> `served`    #a020a685 is the bake above, and every visitor gets it. #1e472bda was yours alone, and is gone

Keeps the side-by-side evidence — which is the payoff — but each hash now has an unmistakable role and one of them is explicitly anchored to the thing they're looking at. Longest of the four, though see the note on cost below.

---

**3. Instrument-terse** — leans on the page's existing `·` idiom

> `compared`    yours #1e472bda — gone · everyone's #a020a685 — above

Highly scannable, and changing the label from `served` to `compared` does real work: it tells you this row is a comparison before you read either hash. Risk: reads as jargon, and drops the sentence rhythm the rest of the panel has.

---

**4. Two rows** — maximum clarity, changes the shape

> `you saw`    #1e472bda — rendered for you, cached for nobody
> `served`     #a020a685 — the bake above, and what every visitor gets

Parallel structure, hashes vertically aligned so the difference is visible rather than read, each one labelled in the column that already exists for labelling. This is the clearest of the four by some distance.

The cost is real: the `dl` gains a row, and to keep the layout stable I'd reserve that row in all three phases — about 24px of empty space at desktop in phases A and B.

---

**On length:** options 1–3 cost nothing. The detail slot already reserves two lines at desktop, so a longer phase-C line fits inside the existing reserve. And because the ghost placeholder is generated from the same template function as the real string, whichever wording you pick keeps its reserve in sync automatically — the test enforces that.

My pick is **2** if you want to keep the current shape, **4** if you'd trade 24px for the clearest version. Tell me which, or mix — e.g. option 4's labels with option 2's phrasing.
